Reinforcement learning: the problems behind the methods

From playing Breaking Bellman to the problems behind reinforcement learning: delayed credit, exploration, scale and learning from guesses.

October 20, 20266 min read

reinforcement-learningmachine-learning

Reinforcement learning

Part 0 of 5

  1. Reinforcement learning: the problems behind the methods
  2. RL methods: a family tree and a Q table
  3. Bootstrapping: learn before the reward arrives
  4. Function approximation: share a value, share an error
  5. On-policy and off-policy: whose future are we learning?
  6. The deadly triad: how a guess can train itself upward
Next: RL methods: a family tree and a Q table →

I started exploring reinforcement learning because of the deadly triad. I learned about RL by playing Breaking Bellman, and I’m sharing what I learn in this series.

The triad combines three useful ideas. We can learn before we know the outcome, share what we learn across situations, and reuse data from another policy. But together, these ideas can create a feedback loop where an error feeds into the next prediction. To understand how that happens, we first need to look at the problems each idea solves.

Part 0. Next: the method tree and a Q table.

In reinforcement learning, we have an agent that takes actions, observes what happens and receives rewards. Its policy is the rule it uses to choose actions. We want the agent to earn more reward over time, but it has to learn which choices will get it there.

The reward arrives late

Suppose you win a game after a hundred moves. You get a final reward, so you know the game went well. But which moves actually contributed to the win? Maybe the last move was obvious, while a choice much earlier made the winning route possible.

Connecting that outcome to the decisions that contributed to it is called credit assignment. The same problem comes up when a robot reaches for an object. Even if it only knows whether it succeeded at the end, it needs to learn about both the approach and the grasp.

We will estimate future reward and use those estimates to carry information back to earlier choices. In Part 1, we can see those estimates in a table.

A good first result can hide a better choice

Imagine you have ten slot machines, and you don’t know their average payouts. You try one and get a good payout. Do you keep playing that machine, or spend some turns trying the others?

If you repeat the choice that looks best so far, that is exploitation. If you try a less familiar choice, that is exploration. The problem is that rewards can be noisy. A lucky first payout might keep you playing a mediocre machine. Exploring has a cost now, but what you learn can help you make better decisions later.

We compare these choices in Part 1’s bandit example, then add states and a longer future to consider.

Waiting for the outcome can be expensive

We could wait until each game ends before learning from it. With a long episode, though, we would be waiting a long time. And that one outcome can depend on many chance events.

With bootstrapping, we combine a reward we have observed with an estimate of what comes next, so we can learn before the final result arrives. Information can travel sooner, but an error in that estimate can also become part of what we learn from next. Part 2 compares waiting, guessing and looking several steps ahead.

There are too many situations to learn separately

In a small grid, we have a manageable number of cells. But with camera images or a robot’s joint positions, there are far more situations than we can visit one by one. If we had to learn a separate answer for each situation, almost everything would remain unknown.

With function approximation, we use a model, such as a neural network, to share learning across situations. Learning from one situation can improve a prediction somewhere else, but it can also change a prediction that was already good. In Part 3, we follow both effects through one shared weight.

The data may come from different choices

A robot might have stored experience collected by an older controller. Or an agent might be taking random actions to explore, while trying to learn how a more decisive policy would behave.

So the policy collecting the data can be different from the policy we want to evaluate. When we use data from one policy to learn about another, that is off-policy learning. With on-policy learning, we evaluate the policy that produces the experience. Reusing data is useful, but we still need enough information about the choices we want to evaluate. If an action was never tried, it can remain unknown. Part 4 shows this difference at the edge of a cliff.

A prediction can feed its own error

Now consider what happens when we combine the three ideas. With bootstrapping, the target we learn toward contains a prediction. With function approximation, one update can change several predictions. Off-policy data can leave some of those predictions without enough correction. So an update can enlarge an error, and the next target can carry that error forward.

We call this combination the deadly triad. It can make learning unstable, although it does not cause every learner using these three ideas to fail. In Part 5, we build the feedback loop using two states and one weight, then look at ways to interrupt it.

The route through the series

  1. The method tree and a Q table: connect methods to their problems, then watch one table learn.
  2. Bootstrapping: choose how much observed reward to use before a guess. This also leads to Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE), which mixes return lengths to assign action credit.
  3. Function approximation: see what changes when predictions share weights.
  4. On-policy and off-policy learning: separate the policy collecting data from the one being evaluated.
  5. The deadly triad: bring the three mechanisms together and examine stability.

We start with these questions. Next, we will look at the tools people developed to answer them.

Sources

The progression draws on Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, second edition: exploration in Chapter 2, returns and policies in Chapter 3, temporal-difference learning in Chapter 6, approximation in Chapter 9 and the deadly triad in Section 11.3. Van Hasselt and colleagues examine the interaction between the triad’s ingredients. The small slot-machine drawing shows how two initial payouts can mislead a greedy choice; the measured comparisons and their settings are in Part 1.
